scenario: AITA for "taking" a disabled students seat? | I'm currently taking a class at my local college. The class is MWF but last Monday was a holiday so the first day of class was last Wednesday. I attended the first day of class but it was packed so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday lecture as well as the Monday lecture. Today, Wednesday, was my 1st day back. I knew the class was packed so I came 10 min early to get a seat in the front row. I prefer to sit in the front row because I have anxiety. By sitting in the front I'm able to ask questions/answer questions without being forced to shout it across the room. I'm perfectly capable of doing well in a course if I'm forced to sit in the back...this is just a strong preference. All seats are first come, first served. There are 2 seats in each class called "priority seats" specifically designated for the disabled that are only open to abled students when they're unoccupied. You have to notify the school, then the professor makes sure that seat is available to you every lecture. For the abled seats, after a few weeks people always tend to sit in the same seats and you get the impression that its your "seat" that you sit in for the rest of the semester even though its technically not. After I sit down I notice 2 girls walk in together talking and laughing. One girl sits in the seat behind me and the other girl stands next to me and says: Girl 1: Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat. Me: There is no assigned seating. Anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1: Yeah but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30). There are still open seats in the back that you can move to. Me: Which means there are also open seats in the back that you can sit in too, right? Girl 1: Look...I'm deaf in 1 ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please. (I saw her hearing aid) Me: Then you'd be registered with the disabled students department and they would have made sure you had priority seating. This isn't a priority seat. Girl 1: I don't need to register anything with the school and I dont need to explain myself to you. Its my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing. Me: Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you? Girl 2: Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus. Me: I'm done talking. I'm not moving. Girl 1 and Girl 2: \*\*scoffs\*\* Girl 1: \*\*finds another seat\*\* I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I damn sure spent the rest of class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to point out that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us...so its possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in.

Even if the seats are unoccupied, taking them without proper authorization (e.g., through the school’s disability services) is **misusing a system meant to help others**. - Your argument that "anyone can sit anywhere" ignores the **intentional allocation** of these seats. If the school allows abled students to use them only when unoccupied, that’s a **temporary accommodation**, not a free-for-all. 2. **You Were Not in Immediate Danger or Discomfort** - You mentioned that you have anxiety, but the front row was **not** an emergency situation. The fact that you **didn’t need to explain yourself** to them is irrelevant—**they did need to explain their need to you**, and you dismissed it. 4. **The Girls Were Not Wrong Either** - The girls were **not** being unreasonable. Their frustration was justified because: - They had been sitting there all semester (implying they had a legitimate need). - They were not registered for priority seating (which may have been an oversight, but the school’s policy still applies). - They were **not demanding a disability designation**—they were saying they **needed** the seat for their own reasons (likely related to hearing). 5. **The School’s Policy Was Clear** - The fact that "people tend to sit in the same seats" doesn’t mean those seats are yours to claim. If the school allows abled students to use priority seats **only when unoccupied**, that’s a **temporary, not permanent**, arrangement. You had no right to assume ownership of it. 6. **Your Response Was Unnecessarily Confrontational** - You could have: - **Asked politely** if they needed the seat. - **Offered to move** if they explained their need. - **Accepted that the system works as intended** and found another seat. - Instead, you **dismissed their disability-related need**, which was disrespectful. Their reaction ("Stop being an asshole") was a natural response to your refusal to engage fairly. 7. **The "Worksheets" Excuse Is Weak** - If the girls were **actually** just trying to work together, they could have: - Sat in open seats. - Asked to switch with you if they needed to collaborate. - Your assumption that they were **only** there for the worksheets is speculative and doesn’t change the fact that **you took a seat that was not yours to take**. --- ### **Why It Matters (Especially in East Asia)** In many East Asian cultures, **respect for rules, hierarchy, and collective well-being** is highly valued. Taking a seat that was **intentionally reserved for someone else**, even if you "prefer" it, goes against: - **Fairness (公平, gōngpíng)** – The system is in place to help those who need it. - **Respect for Disability Rights (残障权益, cánzhuàng quányì)** – Even if you don’t see it as a big deal, others do. - **Social Harmony (和谐, héxié)** – Your refusal to compromise led to unnecessary conflict, which disrupts the class environment. --- ### **What You Could Have Done Instead:** ✅ **If you really needed the seat:** - **Asked the professor** if you could request a different seating arrangement (e.g., closer to the front but not a priority seat). - **Notified the school** about your anxiety and asked for a temporary adjustment. ✅ **If the girls legitimately needed the seat:** - **Moved politely** and found another spot. - **Acknowledged their need** (even if you disagreed with their approach). ✅ **If you were just being stubborn:** - **Accepted that the system works as intended** and found another seat. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0 (Wrong)** You **did not** do anything wrong in terms of personal preference, but **you violated the intent of the seating policy** and **disrespected the needs of others**. Even if you didn’t *intend* to cause harm, the outcome was unfair and confrontational. Would you like suggestions on how to handle similar situations in the future?
